section: Child Development & Pedagogy · Ch10 — Memory & Forgetting
subject: Child Development & Pedagogy
stem: A student glances at a phone number, holds it in mind just long enough to dial it, and then forgets it entirely. This describes the limited-capacity, brief store called:
explanation: Short-term/working memory holds a small amount of information briefly (~7±2 items) unless rehearsed for transfer to long-term storage.

section: Child Development & Pedagogy · Ch10 — Memory & Forgetting
subject: Child Development & Pedagogy
stem: Hermann Ebbinghaus's experiments on nonsense syllables showed that forgetting is:

options.option_text: Steepest immediately after learning, then levels off gradually
A constant, uniform rate across all time intervals
Absent entirely if the material was ever meaningful
Faster for meaningful material than for nonsense material

explanation: The Ebbinghaus forgetting curve shows rapid initial memory loss followed by a slower decline — the basis for spaced revision soon after learning.

section: Child Development & Pedagogy · Ch10 — Memory & Forgetting
subject: Child Development & Pedagogy
stem: A student who has just learned French vocabulary finds it harder to recall German vocabulary learned earlier. This is best explained by:

options.option_text: Retroactive interference — new learning disrupting recall of older learning
Proactive interference — older learning disrupting new learning

explanation: Retroactive interference occurs when newer learning (French) interferes with recall of earlier learning (German). Proactive interference would be the reverse.

subject: Child Development & Pedagogy
stem: The 'Big Five' model describing personality along Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Neuroticism belongs to which broad approach?
explanation: Trait theories (Big Five/OCEAN) describe personality as measurable dimensions present in varying degrees in everyone, unlike type theories which sort people into discrete categories.

subject: Child Development & Pedagogy
stem: In Freud's structural model, the part of personality that operates on the 'pleasure principle', seeking immediate gratification without regard for consequences, is the:
explanation: The id is the primitive, instinct-driven part working on the pleasure principle. The ego operates on the reality principle; the superego represents internalised moral standards.
